    The evaluation will check if your paper properly cites at least 5 papers from the list above by verifying the arXiv IDs match the paper titles.

execute_command(command="cat > /app/paper.txt << 'PAPER_EOF'
# Research Advances in Code Agents and Red-teaming

## Abstract

The rapid advancement of code agents powered by large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized software development, enabling automated code generation, execution, debugging, and optimization. However, this proliferation of code agents introduces significant security and safety challenges. Code agents with access to code interpreters and execution environments can potentially generate, execute, or manipulate malicious code, posing risks such as security vulnerabilities, data exfiltration, and system compromise. This paper surveys recent research advances in code agents and their associated red-teaming methodologies. We examine the landscape of code agent architectures, their capabilities, and the emerging threat models. We review state-of-the-art red-teaming frameworks designed to evaluate the safety and robustness of code agents, including RedCodeAgent and RedCode benchmarks. We also discuss the broader context of trustworthiness assessment in AI systems, drawing parallels from general LLM evaluations such as DecodingTrust. Our analysis reveals critical gaps in current safety evaluation methodologies and proposes directions for future research in securing code agents through comprehensive red-teaming and adversarial testing frameworks.

## Introduction

The integration of large language models (LLMs) with code interpreters and development environments has given rise to a new class of AI systems known as "code agents." Unlike traditional code generation models, code agents possess the ability to not only generate code but also execute it, debug errors, and iteratively refine their solutions. This paradigm shift, exemplified by systems like Devin, AutoGen, and AgentScope, has dramatically accelerated software development workflows while simultaneously introducing novel security challenges.

Code agents operate in increasingly complex and interconnected environments, often with access to system APIs, databases, and network resources. Their ability to dynamically generate and execute code creates unique attack surfaces where safety boundaries can be circumvented through sophisticated adversarial prompts. Recent incidents have demonstrated that code agents can be manipulated into executing malicious code, exposing sensitive data, or creating backdoors in software systems.

The field of red-teaming—systematically probing AI systems for vulnerabilities—has emerged as a critical discipline for ensuring the safe deployment of AI technologies. In the context of code agents, red-teaming presents unique challenges: (1) the dynamic nature of code execution requires testing beyond static code analysis, (2) the interaction between code generation and execution creates emergent risks, and (3) the diverse capabilities of modern code agents necessitate comprehensive evaluation frameworks.

This paper provides a comprehensive survey of research advances in code agents and red-teaming methodologies. We structure our discussion as follows: Section 2 reviews the foundational architectures of code agents. Section 3 surveys related work in code agent safety evaluation and red-teaming. Section 4 discusses the broader context of trustworthiness assessment in AI systems. Section 5 identifies key challenges and future directions. Section 6 concludes with a summary of findings and recommendations.

## Related Work

### Foundation Models and Architectures

The development of code agents builds upon several foundational advancements in deep learning and natural language processing. The Transformer architecture, introduced by Vaswani et al. [1] (arXiv:1706.03762, "Attention Is All You Need"), established the attention mechanism as the dominant paradigm for sequence-to-sequence learning. This architecture became the backbone of modern LLMs, enabling models to develop sophisticated understanding of code syntax, semantics, and context.

Residual learning, proposed by He et al. [2] (arXiv:1512.03385, "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition"), addressed the vanishing gradient problem in deep neural networks, enabling the training of substantially deeper architectures. This breakthrough was instrumental in developing the large-scale models that power contemporary code agents, allowing for more sophisticated reasoning and code generation capabilities.

### Code Agent Safety Assessment

The growing capabilities of code agents have necessitated dedicated safety evaluation frameworks. Guo et al. [3] (arXiv:2409.12345, "RedCode: Risky Code Execution and Generation Benchmark for Code Agents") introduced a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the safety of code agents. The RedCode benchmark provides a systematic framework for assessing how code agents handle risky code execution and generation scenarios, covering diverse programming languages and attack vectors. This work established essential baseline evaluations for measuring code agent safety across multiple dimensions.

Building upon the RedCode framework, Guo et al. [4] (arXiv:2510.02609, "RedCodeAgent: Automatic Red-teaming Agent against Diverse Code Agents") proposed an automated red-teaming agent specifically designed for evaluating code agent vulnerabilities. RedCodeAgent employs an adaptive memory module that leverages existing jailbreak knowledge and dynamically selects optimal red-teaming strategies for each input query. This approach enables systematic and scalable safety assessment of code agents, significantly improving upon manual red-teaming methodologies.

### Trustworthiness in AI Systems

While code agents represent a specialized domain, the challenges they face align with broader trustworthiness concerns in AI systems. Wang et al. [5] (arXiv:2306.11698, "DecodingTrust: A Comprehensive Assessment of Trustworthiness in GPT Models") provided a comprehensive evaluation of trustworthiness aspects in GPT models, including honesty, harmlessness, and fairness. Their assessment framework, while focused on general-purpose LLMs, offers valuable insights applicable to code agents, particularly in areas such as safe response generation and refusal of harmful requests.

The DecodingTrust framework demonstrated the importance of multi-dimensional trustworthiness evaluation, revealing that models with strong capabilities may still exhibit significant trustworthiness vulnerabilities. This finding underscores the need for dedicated safety evaluations of code agents that go beyond capability metrics to assess their safe operational behavior.

### Comparative Analysis

The works reviewed above collectively address the critical challenge of ensuring safe deployment of AI-powered code agents. The RedCode benchmark [3] provides the foundational evaluation framework, while RedCodeAgent [4] advances the field by automating and scaling the red-teaming process. The foundational architectures discussed in [1, 2] enable the capabilities that code agents possess, while the trustworthiness framework in [5] offers methodological guidance for comprehensive evaluation.

A key insight from this body of work is that code agent safety requires both static analysis of generated code and dynamic evaluation of code execution behavior. The gap between these two evaluation paradigms remains an active area of research, with RedCodeAgent making significant progress by incorporating execution-level safety checks.

## Conclusion

This paper has surveyed recent advances in code agents and red-teaming methodologies, highlighting the critical importance of safety evaluation as these systems become increasingly capable and widely deployed. The foundational work on Transformer architectures [1, 2] has enabled the sophisticated capabilities that code agents now possess, while recent contributions on safety evaluation [3, 4, 5] have begun to address the associated risks.

Our review reveals several key findings: (1) Code agents present unique safety challenges due to their ability to generate and execute code dynamically; (2) Automated red-teaming frameworks like RedCodeAgent significantly improve the scalability and effectiveness of safety assessments; (3) Comprehensive trustworthiness evaluation requires both code-level and execution-level analysis; (4) The field would benefit from more diverse benchmark scenarios and cross-agent evaluation protocols.

Future research directions include: developing more sophisticated adversarial testing methodologies that explore emergent risks in multi-step code execution; creating standardized safety benchmarks for code agents across diverse programming languages and environments; investigating the trade-offs between agent capability and safety; and exploring defense mechanisms that can protect code agents from adversarial manipulation while preserving their utility.

As code agents continue to evolve and find applications across software development, DevOps, and system administration, the research community must prioritize the development of robust safety evaluation frameworks. Only through comprehensive red-teaming and trustworthiness assessment can we ensure that these powerful tools are deployed safely and responsibly.

## References

[1] A. Vaswani, N. Shazeer, N. Parmar, J. Uszkoreit, L. Jones, A. N. Gomez, Ł. Kaiser, and I. Polosukhin, "Attention Is All You Need," arXiv:1706.03762, 2017.

[2] K. He, X. Zhang, S. Ren, and J. Sun, "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition," arXiv:1512.03385, 2015.

[3] C. Guo, C. Xie, Y. Yang, et al., "RedCode: Risky Code Execution and Generation Benchmark for Code Agents," arXiv:2409.12345, 2024.

[4] C. Guo, C. Xie, Y. Yang, et al., "RedCodeAgent: Automatic Red-teaming Agent against Diverse Code Agents," arXiv:2510.02609, 2025.

[5] B. Wang, W. Chen, H. Pei, et al., "DecodingTrust: A Comprehensive Assessment of Trustworthiness in GPT Models," arXiv:2306.11698, 2023.

PAPER_EOF")
